articles.title: Russian director refuses to denounce lead actor despite criticism from Ukraine
articles.summary: Ilya Khrzhanovsky’s DAU, about physicist Lev Landau, stars Russian conductor Teodor Currentzis, who has refused to speak out against Putin’s war. The director of a controversial new Russian film has said “everyone pays for his own choice” when asked about his lead’s refusal to condemn Russia’s war…
body: In film-maker Ilya Khrzhanovsky’s DAU, which premiered at the Venice film festival on Wednesday, Greek-Russian star conductor Teodor Currentzis plays the eponymously nicknamed protagonist, Nobel prize-winning quantum physicist Lev Landau.

In the run-up to the festival, the film’s inclusion in the lineup was heavily criticised by the Ukrainian ministry of foreign affairs, in part over the fact that Athens-born Currentzis continues to live and work in Russia, and has never publicly denounced Putin’s war.

“It’s his choice,” Khrzhanovsky said at a press conference on the Lido. “But I think everyone is paying for his own choice, his own life, his own destiny,” added the film-maker, who has renounced his Russian citizenship over the full-scale invasion and lives in exile in Germany.

He referred to his film, in which Currentzis’s character Landau is put under pressure to work on the development of the nuclear bomb and eventually reluctantly agrees. “As you can see in the movie, the main character is also making different choices, and he’s paying for his choices.”

articles.title: Union Town review – passionate exposé of US delivery workers’ employment conditions
articles.summary: Venice film festival: Barbara Kopple returns with her third film investigating US workers’ rights – this time, undocumented ‘deliveristas’ and the attempts to unionise Amazon staff.
body: Barbara Kopple’s documentary about app-based delivery workers is a stirring, defiant, battle-hardened affair, swinging between the fraught picket line and the still more hazardous New York City streets. It’s a new film that feels old in the best sense of the word; a hoarse battle cry that summons the ghosts of The Grapes of Wrath and the New Deal, Eugene Debs and Woody Guthrie. That America is long dead and buried, a casualty of changing times, but Kopple sees no reason why it should not rise again.

articles.title: John Malkovich cancels Israel trip over fabricated solidarity quote
articles.summary: The Wild Horse Nine actor had been due to appear on stage in The Music Critic in Tel Aviv – but pulled out over PR firm’s ‘unacceptable and untenable’ attribution of statement.
body: John Malkovich has cancelled a planned trip to Israel next year to appear on stage after a PR firm hired by the show attributed quotes to the actor that the company had written.

Malkovich, who is a leading Oscar contender for his role in Martin McDonagh’s Wild Horse Nine, was due to appear in The Music Critic, a theatrical-musical satire composed by the Jewish violinist Aleksey Igudesman, in Tel Aviv’s Charles Bronfman Auditorium on 13 April.

A press release circulated on 5 September quoted Malkovich as saying he was “thrilled to return to Israel” and looked “forward to meeting the warm Israeli audience once again, to whom I feel a strong closeness and solidarity”.

The actor, 72, was alerted to the quotes after reading them in the Hollywood Reporter, who picked them up from the Jerusalem Post. In a statement to the Hollywood Reporter on 8 September, Malkovich said that a “PR company hired by the Israeli promoter drafted a quote for the article that was attributed to me, though I never made the statements that were quoted, nor was I consulted before they were printed.”

articles.title: The Uprising review – the peasants are revolting in muddled historical epic
articles.summary: Andrew Garfield’s charisma can’t save Paul Greengrass’s grim and depressingly generic period piece. Hollywood loves giving young actors their own historical epic as much as audiences seem to dislike watching them.
body: On paper, The Uprising should be different: it’s a historical epic from a blue-chip director (the Bourne trilogy’s Paul Greengrass ), a nuanced, introspective leading man ( Andrew Garfield ) and a milieu that uncomfortably chimes with the western world’s backslide into repressive authoritarianism (The Peasants’ Revolt of 1381). In reality, it is a disjointed slog through the mud with the emotional depth of a History Channel rerun.

Thus follows a rather hectic-feeling race from one greige setting to the next as the rebels have their run of modern-day Kent, assembling in Maidstone before storming Canterbury cathedral, and then traveling to meet the king and his men in Blackheath. Greengrass’s camerawork can occasionally swoon, with stunning aerial shots of a flotilla on the Thames, but his signature handheld style is a trick that has gone stale: the only uprising I felt during the seasick fight scenes was my breakfast threatening to return on me.
points: Andrew Garfield’s charisma can’t save Paul Greengrass’s grim and depressingly generic period piece.
Hollywood loves giving young actors their own historical epic as much as audiences seem to dislike watching them.

articles.title: ‘RuPaul’s Drag Race UK: All Stars’ Set to Premiere on WOW Presents Plus (EXCLUSIVE)
articles.summary: “RuPaul’s Drag Race UK” is moving from the BBC and headed to World of Wonder‘s streaming platform WOW Presents Plus. The news comes after The Sun reported that the show would be leaving the BBC as part of its cuts.
body: The show’s eighth season, which just launched on BBC 3 scored its second-highest-rated premiere in the history of the franchise, trailing only Season 6 (which scored 9.0). The show bowed to an 8.8 IMDB rating with viewership up 20% on the streaming platform WOW Presents Plus.
The successful launch of Season 8 follows a record-breaking run of the global franchise.

The main show, “RuPaul’s Drag Race,” recently finished its 18th season and was the most watched season in the franchise’s history. Myki Meeks didn’t have the strongest start to the season, but after her fellow queens placed her at the bottom of the “Rate-A-Queen” twist, she exacted her revenge. In the end, it was Meeks who sashayed her way to the top and was crowned the winner of “RuPaul’s Drag Race” Season 18. The show also landed 11 Emmy nominations for Season 18 and its aftershow, “RuPaul’s Drag Race: Untucked.”

The franchise continued to expand and grow with new seasons and formats of “Canada’s Drag Race,” “Drag Race Down Under,” “Drag Race Mexico” and “Drag Race France.” All premiered with significant double digit growth.

articles.title: Newly Discovered Plant-Eating Insects Named After Taylor Swift
articles.summary: Taylor Swift, the award-winning billionaire singer and songwriter, is getting a new honor: The megastar is the namesake of several recently discovered species of plant-feeding insects from Australia.
body: The Swiftiephylus insects are closely associated with Australian she-oaks, trees and shrubs adapted to environments ranging from tropical forests to coastal dunes and extreme heat, according to UC Riverside. Many plant bugs spend their entire lives on a particular host plant, from hatching through adulthood and egg laying.

UC Riverside entomology doctoral student Sarah Schroeder decided to name the insects after Swift, in the hopes her association with the bugs will elevate both the insects and the concept of insect conservation more generally. “It felt authentic to me as a lifelong Swiftie to honor Taylor in this way, as well as bring attention to the diversity of insects that has yet to be discovered,” Schroeder said in a statement provided by the university.

articles.title: Actor Noel Clarke charged with sexual offences
articles.summary: Clarke has been charged with offences including sexual assault. BBC News has asked him for a comment.
body: Actor Noel Clarke has been charged with sexual offences including sexual assault, voyeurism and exposure.
The Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) authorised the Metropolitan Police to charge the Doctor Who and Kidulthood star on Wednesday.

Clarke, 50, from Kensington, west London, was charged with two counts of sexual assault, three charges of voyeurism and one charge of exposure. The offences are alleged to have taken place between 2007 and 2016 and relate to five women.

In a statement released on Wednesday, the CPS said: "Our prosecutors have worked to establish that there is sufficient evidence to bring this case to court and that it is in the public interest to do so."

articles.title: ‘Holy Wood Dust’ Review: Victor Kossakovsky’s Soothing, if Slightly Dull, Documentary Will Make You Want to Hug a Tree
articles.summary: Playing out of competition in Venice, the latest from the 'Gunda' and 'Architecton' helmer is a meditation on the precious beauty and importance of trees.
body: Cinematic lyrical poet Victor Kossakovsky ( Architecton, Gunda ) offers in Holy Wood Dust another distinctive non-fiction meditation on a theme, a work that’s eloquent even if the author’s message is not always explicitly articulated. This time the subject is trees, mostly living ones growing, or at least trying to grow, around the Dolomites in Northern Italy — though the focus broadens to incorporate trees grown on an industrial scale for the Christmas season, especially in Germany.

Things have recently gotten a little spicier and more innovative in the nature documentary space, making this feel a bit old-school compared to, say Jesse McLean’s wonderful Light Needs, an experimental work about indoor plants that literally gives our potted pals voices, or the recent kaleidoscopic crowd-sourced feature Super Nature by Ed Sayers. French doc Heart of an Oak from a few years back, on the other hand, is comparatively less formally innovative, but by focusing on just the one tree and getting stuck right in to how that forms a micro-ecosystem on its own, it feels more cohesive and rich in factoids than the wafty approach allows here.
points: Playing out of competition in Venice, the latest from the 'Gunda' and 'Architecton' helmer is a meditation on the precious beauty and importance of trees.

articles.title: How Hollywood Shapes Our Understanding of Health
articles.summary: A study sponsored by Eli Lilly and Company (Lilly) shows that chronic illness is historically underrepresented on screen, while a growing coalition of studios, researchers, and patient advocates work to change that reality.
body: Film and TV have always shaped how audiences see the world. Movies and shows have transformed how people think about mental health, addiction, sexuality, and countless other topics once considered too private for the big screen. But when it comes to one of the most common parts of our daily lives—living with illness—many of today’s most prevalent chronic diseases are still largely missing from popular entertainment.

For the millions of people living with a health condition, or caring for someone who is, on-screen portrayals matter much more than viewers realize. Authentic representation of illness can influence awareness, chip away at stigma, and ultimately shape health outcomes. As a medicine company that puts health above all, Lilly has supported research and collaborations designed to help the entertainment industry depict the lived experience of disease with greater authenticity, empathy, and nuance.
